sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Ever tried to calculate something huge—like the number of atoms in the universe—and Java just gave up? Let’s fix that!

• How to handle numbers bigger than `long` can hold
• Why `BigInteger` and `BigDecimal` are your new best friends
• When to use them (and when to stick with `int`/`double`)

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine you’re counting grains of sand on a beach. A regular calculator (like `int` or `double`) would run out of digits fast—just like you’d run out of fingers!

`BigInteger` and `BigDecimal` are like super-powered calculators that never run out of space. They handle:

• **`BigInteger`**: Whole numbers of *any* size (even 1000 digits long!)
  - Perfect for cryptography, factorials, or counting stars

• **`BigDecimal`**: Precise decimal numbers (no more `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004` nonsense!)
  - Essential for money, scientific calculations, or exact measurements

**Why not just use `double`?**
- `double` is like a rubber ruler—it stretches but loses accuracy
- `BigDecimal` is like a metal ruler—precise but slower (trade-off!)

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ `BigInteger` = Whole numbers with *no size limit* (use for cryptography, huge counts)
✓ `BigDecimal` = Precise decimals (use for money, science, or exact math)
✓ Both are *immutable*—every operation returns a new object (like `String`)

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Initialize with *strings* to avoid precision loss (e.g., `"0.1"` not `0.1`)
donts: Don’t assume `BigDecimal` is always precise (set scale for rounding!)
sections.protip: For `BigDecimal`, always set a *scale* and *rounding mode* (e.g., `setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)`) to avoid surprises!

problem.description:
Write a program that calculates the factorial of 50 (50!). Regular `int` or `long` will overflow—use `BigInteger` instead!

Bonus: Format the output to group digits (e.g., 3,041,409...).
hints: Start with `BigInteger.ONE` and multiply in a loop
problem.explanation: We start with `1` (as a `BigInteger`) and multiply it by every number from 1 to 50. The `String.format` adds commas for readability—just like a calculator!

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 Use them for money, science, or huge numbers—otherwise, stick to `int`/`double`
📌 Ready to tackle real-world math problems without limits!
